nameStory: The Redlined Wolf Spider gets its name from the distinctive reddish markings that often appear along its body, creating subtle "red lines" that help distinguish it from other wolf spiders. Like all wolf spiders, it's called a "wolf" spider because it actively hunts its prey rather than building webs to catch food, prowling the ground like a tiny predator.
description: The Redlined Wolf Spider is a medium-sized ground-dwelling hunter with a robust, hairy body typical of wolf spiders. These spiders have excellent eyesight thanks to their prominent forward-facing eyes, which they use to spot prey and potential mates. They're built for speed and agility, with strong legs that help them chase down insects across sandy or rocky terrain. Adults typically reach about half an inch in body length, not counting their legs.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes arranged in a square pattern on top of the head, with the front pair noticeably larger and more prominent - they almost seem to be looking right at you with an alert, intelligent expression

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Subtle reddish or rusty-colored lines or patches on the brownish body, often most visible on the cephalothorax (front body section) - the markings may appear faded or worn in older individuals

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, robust build with a hairy texture that feels slightly fuzzy if gently touched - the body appears flattened and built for hugging close to the ground

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Runs in quick bursts across open ground when disturbed, often stopping suddenly to assess threats - females may be seen carrying a round, whitish egg sac attached to their spinnerets

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Does not build webs for catching prey, but may create a simple silk-lined burrow or retreat under rocks and debris

habitat: Look for Redlined Wolf Spiders in sandy or gravelly areas near streams, rivers, and lakeshores throughout New England. They prefer open, sunlit spots with loose soil or small rocks where they can easily burrow or hide. You might spot them along hiking trails, in clearings, or near the edges of wooded areas where the canopy opens up.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and become active hunters. Males begin searching for mates and may be seen wandering more openly during daylight hours.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both hunting and mating behaviors are most visible. Females carrying white egg sacs are commonly observed during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Spiderlings disperse and adults prepare for winter by seeking shelter under rocks, logs, or in shallow burrows. Activity decreases as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in protected locations like rock crevices or under deep leaf litter, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Female Redlined Wolf Spiders are devoted mothers who carry their egg sacs attached to their bodies for weeks, and when the babies hatch, they climb onto mom's back and ride around like tiny passengers on a living bus until they're big enough to hunt on their own!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other wolf spiders in the Arctosa genus, especially the Shoreline Wolf Spider. Remember "Red for Redlined" - look for those subtle reddish markings that give this species its name, while Shoreline Wolf Spiders typically lack these rusty tones.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name "Arctosa" means "bear-like," referring to these spiders' stocky, robust build and hairy appearance that somewhat resembles a tiny bear. Despite being called wolf spiders, they're completely harmless to humans and actually beneficial for controlling pest insects.
compareHints: Among the Arctosa genus, the Redlined Wolf Spider is distinguished by its reddish markings, while the Shoreline Wolf Spider tends to be grayer and is more strictly coastal in habitat. Emerton's Wolf Spider is typically darker overall without the characteristic reddish lines. All three share the same basic body plan and eye arrangement, but the subtle color differences and habitat preferences help separate them.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the bear spiders (Arctosa genus), the Shoreline Wolf Spider is distinguished by its strict coastal habitat preference, while the Redlined Wolf Spider has more pronounced reddish markings and Emerton's Wolf Spider tends to be found in drier, inland sandy areas.
Emerton's Wolf Spider is distinguished from its close relatives the Shoreline Wolf Spider and Redlined Wolf Spider primarily by habitat preference and subtle differences in markings.
